title: Barrier-free access for mobility scooters and wheelchairs on public footpaths
asked: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong asked what measures are being taken to ensure all public footpaths, including roadside footpaths in private estates, provide barrier-free access for mobility scooters and motorised wheelchairs, so users are not forced onto roads and risk safety or prosecution under the Active Mobility Act 2017.
response: Mr Baey Yam Keng said public paths are designed to be free from encumbrances, and since 2018 new standalone footpaths must have a minimum clear width of 1.8 metres, while those next to cycling paths must be at least 1.5 metres. Old footpaths will be widened to these standards when rejuvenated unless site constraints such as lack of roadside space apply. LTA takes residents' feedback for footpath widening in private estates, often alongside drainage or estate improvements, and enforcement authorities will exercise discretion if riders briefly use the road to bypass obstructions. He also reminded device users and motorists to slow down in residential estates.

key_points.point: Public paths are designed to be free from encumbrances to ensure barrier-free passage.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: Public paths are designed to be free from encumbrances to ensure a barrier-free passage.

key_points.point: Since 2018, new standalone footpaths must have a minimum clear width of 1.8 metres, and those adjacent to cycling paths at least 1.5 metres.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: Since 2018, all new standalone footpaths are also required to have a minimum clear width of 1.8 metres, while those adjacent to cycling paths must be at least 1.5 metres.

key_points.point: Old footpaths will be widened to these standards when rejuvenated, unless there are site constraints such as lack of roadside space.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: When rejuvenating old footpaths, we will widen them to these standards, unless there are site constraints, such as the lack of roadside space.

key_points.point: LTA takes residents' feedback when planning footpath widening within private estates, often alongside drainage or estate improvements.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) also takes in residents' feedback when planning for footpath widening within private estates, which is often undertaken in conjunction with other programmes, such as drainage or estate improvements.

key_points.point: Enforcement authorities will exercise discretion if riders need to use the road briefly to bypass obstructions or access adjoining paths.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: If riders need to use the road briefly to bypass obstructions or access adjoining paths, enforcement authorities will exercise discretion.

key_points.point: Device users and motorists are reminded to slow down and exercise greater caution in residential estates.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: We would also like to remind device users and motorists to slow down at residential estates and exercise greater caution during such instances.

key_points.point: Path widening work is usually taken with other estate improvement works and is not entirely within LTA's jurisdiction.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: As mentioned earlier, such path widening work is usually taken in conjunction with other estate improvement works, for example, drainage or estate improvements and these are not entirely within LTA's jurisdiction.

key_points.point: Private estates have constraints such as trees and utilities that make widening less straightforward.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: We really have to bear in mind the constraints in private estates, because you have trees, utilities and it is not so straightforward as in other places.

key_points.point: A calibrated approach is taken based on the volume of users, whether motorists on roads or pedestrians and riders on footpaths.
key_points.speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
key_points.quote: We do take a calibrated approach, looking at the volume of users – whether motorists on the roads or pedestrians and riders on the footpaths.

left_open: A specific timeline for when footpaths in private estates that have not been upgraded will be modified.
Whether all roadside footpaths in private estates will be made barrier-free.
How the risk of prosecution under the Active Mobility Act 2017 for PMA users who need to use the road is addressed.
supplementary: Timeline and feasibility for modifying blocked footpaths in older private estates so PMA users need not use the road.
